items.title: The Health Belief Model predicts (some) preventive behaviours
items.claim: Rosenstock's 1974 Health Belief Model proposes that preventive behaviour depends on perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits and barriers. What's its empirical track record?

options.text: It predicts all health behaviours perfectly

Meta-analyses (Carpenter 2010) find modest predictive power: perceived barriers strongest, perceived benefits moderate, susceptibility and severity weaker. The model under-weights social and emotional factors
It only applies to dental hygiene

items.reveal:
Rosenstock developed the HBM from 1950s public health work on TB screening uptake. It has been applied to vaccination, screening, smoking cessation and COVID behaviours.

Competitors and extensions: Theory of Planned Behavior (Ajzen 1991, adds intention and perceived control); Transtheoretical Model (Prochaska 1979, stages of change). Behavioural economics (EAST framework: easy, attractive, social, timely) is the more recent UK policy framework.
items.why: Behaviour-change theories provide testable frameworks but rarely explain more than a fraction of variance. Combining them with structural interventions usually outperforms either alone.

items.title: What we know about Little Albert
items.claim: John Watson and Rosalie Rayner's 1920 'Little Albert' study conditioned an infant to fear a white rat. What is now believed about the child's identity?

options.text: His identity was always public knowledge
Later researchers proposed identifications but no consensus exists
He grew up to become a famous psychologist
Records confirm he kept the conditioned fear for life

items.reveal:
Beck, Levinson and Irons (2009) proposed Douglas Merritte; Powell et al. (2014) proposed William Barger. The case remains unresolved.

The study itself would not meet modern ethical standards for research with infants.
items.why: Ethical reviews now prevent such studies. Their existence in the historical record shapes how we teach research ethics today.

items.title: Eyewitness memories can be planted
items.claim: Elizabeth Loftus's lab implanted entirely false childhood memories in adult participants. What proportion came to believe the fake event was real?
items.reveal_title: About a quarter of people 'remembered' something that never happened
items.reveal:
In the 'Lost in the Mall' study (Loftus & Pickrell, 1995), 25% of participants came to recall a fabricated childhood event after being told by a family member it had occurred.

Later work with more vivid scenarios reached implantation rates around 50%.
items.why: Memory feels like recording. It is reconstruction, and reconstruction is suggestible.
